knowledge_base.What is the difference between Pending,:
Project and work order statuses indicate the current state:
 (1) Pending: Work has not yet started, Resources are being allocated, Waiting for prerequisites (materials, permits, approvals), Vendor has been notified but not mobilized, No field activity has begun, SLA clock may not have started yet (depends on configuration).
 (2) In Progress: Active work is underway, Vendor team is on site or actively working, Materials have been deployed, Progress is being made toward completion, Status updates are being provided, SLA clock is running, May include substates like '25% complete', '50% complete', '75% complete'.
 (3) Completed: All physical work on site is finished, Vendor has submitted Certificate of Completion (COC), May be awaiting QI inspection or already inspected and passed, All required documentation is submitted or being finalized, Project is in billing or closeout phase, No further field work required (unless inspection fails). Additional statuses:
 (4) On Hold: Work temporarily suspended, Waiting for external factors (customer decision, material availability, permit approval), SLA clock may be paused (if valid hold reason), Will resume when hold condition is resolved.
 (5) Cancelled: Project has been cancelled and will not be completed, May be due to customer cancellation, scope change, or other reasons, Resources are freed for other work, Documentation explaining cancellation reason is required.
 (6) Delayed: Work started but is behind schedule, Missed original target completion date, Delay factors must be documented, May have penalties depending on who is responsible for delay, Revised completion date is set. Statuses can be filtered in all project views, and status changes are logged with timestamp and user for audit trail.
knowledge_base.How are priorities assigned to projects?:
Projects are assigned priority levels to help teams focus on the most important work first. Priority levels are:
 (1) Critical (Highest Priority): Emergency situations, safety hazards, or outages affecting customers, Restoration work after storms or natural disasters, Projects with regulatory deadlines or compliance requirements, High-impact failures requiring immediate resolution, VIP customer issues that cannot wait, Work affecting critical infrastructure or multiple customers, Expected completion: Immediate to 24 hours.
 (2) High Priority: Important projects with tight deadlines, Large commercial or industrial customer projects, Projects with contractual deadlines approaching, Work affecting service quality for significant customer base, Projects requested by senior management, Follow-up to critical issues that are partially resolved, Expected completion: 1-3 days.
 (3) Medium Priority (Standard): Routine projects with standard timelines, Normal business work orders, Projects with adequate time before deadline, Scheduled maintenance and upgrades, Standard customer requests, Majority of projects fall into this category, Expected completion: 1-2 weeks.
 (4) Low Priority: Non-urgent improvement projects, Enhancements with flexible timelines, Work that can be done during low-activity periods, Projects awaiting budget approval, Nice-to-have upgrades, Projects that can be postponed if higher priorities arise, Expected completion: Flexible, as resources permit. Priority determines: Order in work queues and dashboards, Speed of resource allocation, SLA timeline expectations, Escalation urgency, Management attention and reporting frequency. Priority can be changed if circumstances change (e.g., customer complaint escalates a project from Medium to High). Team Leaders and Sector Managers have authority to adjust priority based on business needs.

knowledge_base.What is the ML model and how does it hel:
The system includes Machine Learning (ML) models that learn from historical data to make predictions and improve decision-making:
 (1) Delay Prediction Model: Analyzes project characteristics (status, priority, contract value, vendor history, days since start, risk factors), Compares to historical patterns of delayed projects, Predicts probability of delay (Low risk <40%, Medium risk 40-70%, High risk >70%), Identifies which projects need proactive attention, Helps managers intervene early before delays occur, Continuously learns from new project outcomes to improve accuracy.
 (2) Penalty Amount Prediction Model: Takes into account violation type (SLA breach, quality issue, safety violation, documentation issue), Considers delay duration in days, Analyzes contract value and project scope, Reviews vendor's past performance and compliance history, Compares to similar past penalty cases, Suggests appropriate penalty amount based on precedents, Ensures consistency in penalty enforcement across similar violations, Helps avoid penalties that are too harsh or too lenient.
 (3) QI Workload Optimization: Analyzes each QI's historical performance and capacity, Predicts how many inspections a QI can handle per day/week, Considers travel time, project complexity, and inspection types, Suggests optimal inspection assignments to balance workload, Identifies when QI team is overloaded and needs help, Helps set realistic daily targets based on actual capability.
 (4) Resource Allocation Predictions: Predicts which teams will be overloaded in coming weeks, Forecasts when bottlenecks will occur in workflow stages, Suggests reallocation of resources to prevent delays, Helps planning team capacity and hiring needs. Benefits of ML models:
 (1) Proactive instead of reactive - predict and prevent issues before they occur,
 (2) Data-driven decisions - based on actual historical patterns, not just intuition,
 (3) Consistency - apply similar treatment to similar situations,
 (4) Learning - models improve over time as more data is collected,
 (5) Efficiency - automate complex calculations that would take humans significant time,
 (6) Fairness - reduce bias by basing decisions on objective historical data. The models run automatically in the background and their predictions are displayed in relevant dashboards and reports. Users don't need to understand ML to benefit from it - the system presents predictions in simple, actionable terms (e.g., 'High risk of delay', 'Suggested penalty: ₱75,000'). Model accuracy is monitored and models are retrained periodically as new data accumulates.

knowledge_base.What is risk scoring and how is project:
Risk scoring assesses the likelihood that a project will encounter delays, quality issues, or other problems. Each project receives a risk score from 0 to 10: 0-3 (Low Risk - Green): Project progressing normally, Vendor has good track record, All milestones on schedule, Resources adequate, No major concerns. 4-7 (Medium Risk - Yellow): Some minor delays or concerns, Vendor has mixed performance history, Approaching deadlines, Some resource constraints, Needs monitoring. 8-10 (High Risk - Red): Significant likelihood of delay or failure, Vendor has poor performance history, Already behind schedule, Major constraints or issues, Needs immediate intervention. Risk score is calculated based on multiple factors:
 (1) Project Characteristics: Complexity of work (simple vs. complex installations), Contract value (higher value = higher risk impact), Duration and timeline (tight deadlines increase risk), Number of dependencies (waiting on permits, materials, etc.), Technical challenges involved.
 (2) Vendor Performance: Vendor's overall compliance score, Recent project completion track record, History of delays with similar projects, Penalty history and frequency, Current workload and capacity.
 (3) Current Status: Days since project start vs. planned duration, Percentage of work completed vs. timeline, Number and severity of issues encountered so far, Outstanding dependencies or blockers, SLA compliance on this project.
 (4) External Factors: Season (rainy season increases risk), Location accessibility and challenges, Permit approval complexity, Material availability issues, Coordination requirements with other utilities.
 (5) Team Factors: Experience of assigned team members, Workload of QI and supervisors, Availability of required skilled labor, Equipment and resource availability. The risk score is: Calculated automatically when project is created, Recalculated daily as factors change, Displayed on project dashboard with color coding, Used to prioritize management attention, Factored into resource allocation decisions. High-risk projects trigger: More frequent status check-ins, Earlier escalation thresholds, Proactive management review, Additional oversight and support, Contingency planning. The risk score helps managers focus their limited time on projects most likely to need intervention, rather than monitoring all projects equally. Historical risk scores are analyzed to improve the prediction model - if a project scored low risk but still had problems, the model learns from that to improve future predictions.
knowledge_base.What happens during the QI inspection pr:
The Quality Inspection (QI) process is a critical step that verifies work completion before billing. Here's the detailed flow:
 (1) Pre-Inspection: Vendor completes physical work on site, Vendor submits Certificate of Completion (COC) with photos through portal, System automatically notifies assigned QI of COC submission, QI reviews submitted COC and photos in preparation, QI schedules inspection date and time (must be within 3 days SLA), Vendor receives notification of scheduled inspection with date, time, and QI contact, Day before inspection: automatic reminder sent to vendor and QI.
 (2) On-Site Inspection Day: QI travels to project site with inspection equipment and tools, QI meets with vendor representative on site, QI reviews the completed work against project requirements and specifications, QI conducts systematic inspection using checklist.
 (3) Inspection Checklist Items (varies by project type): Verify work matches approved design and specifications, Check materials used meet specifications, Verify proper installation techniques were followed, Test functionality of installations (voltage tests, continuity, grounding, etc.), Check safety requirements (clearances, protective equipment, signage), Verify no damage to surrounding property or utilities, Check workmanship quality and finish, Verify all required materials and components are present, Confirm measurements and dimensions are correct.
 (4) Documentation During Inspection: QI takes photos of completed work from multiple angles, Photos should show key components, connections, and overall installation, QI records measurements and test results, QI marks each checklist item as: Pass (✓) - Meets requirements, Fail (✗) - Does not meet requirements, needs correction, Not Applicable (N/A) - Item doesn't apply to this project type, Conditional Pass (△) - Minor issues that need correction but don't prevent approval.
 (5) Inspection Results: Pass - All items acceptable: QI approves the work immediately, Project can proceed to billing, Vendor notified of successful inspection, COC marked as approved in system, Final documentation package prepared. Fail - Critical defects found: QI documents all deficiencies and issues, Photos taken of problem areas, QI specifies required corrective actions, Deadline set for corrections (typically 3-7 days), Vendor notified with detailed findings, Re-inspection scheduled after corrections, Project billing is blocked until issues resolved, Delay may result in penalties if vendor's fault. Conditional Pass - Minor issues: Work generally acceptable but minor corrections needed, Issues are not critical to functionality or safety, Vendor given specific list of minor corrections, Corrections can be done while billing proceeds, OR Corrections required before final billing depending on severity.
 (6) Post-Inspection: QI submits inspection report through the system within same day or next business day, Report includes: Inspection result (Pass/Fail/Conditional), Detailed findings and comments, Photos with captions explaining what they show, Test results and measurements, Required corrective actions if any, Estimated time for corrections, Re-inspection date if needed. Report is automatically sent to: Vendor (so they know what to correct), Supervisor (for awareness and follow-up), Project team (to proceed with next steps).
 (7) Re-Inspection (if work failed initial inspection): Vendor corrects identified deficiencies, Vendor may upload photos of corrections through portal, QI schedules re-inspection, Re-inspection focuses on previously failed items, If re-inspection passes: Work approved and project proceeds, If re-inspection fails again: Further corrections required, may escalate to management, multiple failures may increase penalties.
 (8) QI Performance Tracking: Each inspection completion updates QI metrics: Daily target achievement (did QI complete expected number of inspections), Average time from COC to inspection (should be under 3 days), Pass/fail rate (indication of vendor quality or QI thoroughness), Re-inspection rate (how often work fails first inspection), Inspection accuracy (are findings valid and consistent). The QI inspection is crucial because: It ensures quality and safety before energization, It verifies vendor actually completed work as contracted, It protects MERALCO from liability for substandard work, It provides objective assessment before payment is released, It maintains quality standards across all vendors, It identifies and corrects issues before they cause problems for customers.
knowledge_base.How does the system handle multiple user:
Vendor companies can have multiple user accounts with different access levels. Here's how it works:
 (1) Primary Account Setup: When vendor is first registered, a primary account is created for the company owner or authorized representative, Primary user receives admin privileges for their company, Primary user can access all features and all projects for their company.
 (2) Adding Additional Users: Primary user or admin logs into Vendor Portal, Goes to User Management or Team Members section, Clicks 'Add User' or 'Invite Team Member', Enters new user details: Full name, Email address, Mobile number, Role/Position in company, Access level to assign. Sends invitation email with temporary login credentials.
 (3) Access Levels for Vendor Users: Admin (Full Access): Can view all company projects, Upload and manage all documents, Submit and manage disputes, View all invoices and payments, Manage other user accounts, Update company profile and contacts, Full access to all portal features. Document Manager: Can upload documents for all projects, View document status and feedback, Receive document-related notifications, Cannot manage penalties or invoices, Cannot add/remove other users. Project Viewer: Can view project information and status, Can download shared documents, Receives notifications about assigned projects, Read-only access, cannot upload or submit, Cannot view financial information or penalties. Field Coordinator: Can upload documents for specific assigned projects only, Can view inspection schedules for their projects, Can receive mobile notifications, Can upload photos from the field, Limited to specific project scope. Finance Officer: Can view invoices and payments, Can download payment documents, Can view penalty information, Cannot upload project documents, Cannot manage users.
 (4) User Assignment to Projects: Admin can assign specific users to specific projects, Assigned users receive notifications only for their projects, Users only see projects they are assigned to (unless they have Admin level), Helps large vendors organize workload across their team.
 (5) User Activity Tracking: System logs which vendor user performed each action, Audit trail shows who uploaded each document, Login history for security monitoring, Activity reports available to vendor admin.
 (6) User Management Features: Admin can deactivate user accounts (if employee leaves), Admin can reset passwords for their team members, Admin can change user access levels as needed, Admin can see last login time for each user.
 (7) Notifications for Multiple Users: Admins can set who receives which notifications, Critical notifications can go to multiple users, Different users can subscribe to different notification types, Helps ensure coverage (if one person away, others still notified).
 (8) Security for Multiple Users: Each user has their own unique login credentials, Actions are tied to individual users, not company account, Password requirements apply to all users, Session management prevents account sharing.
 (9) Benefits of Multiple Users: Large vendors can distribute workload among staff, Field teams can upload documents directly from sites, Office staff can handle billing and disputes separately, Better coverage if key personnel are unavailable, Clear accountability for who did what.
 (10) Limits and Controls: MERALCO may limit total number of users per vendor (e.g., max 10 users), Inactive users may be automatically disabled after period of no login, Suspicious activity triggers security alerts. This system allows vendors to operate efficiently while maintaining clear accountability and security.
knowledge_base.What are the different document types an:
The system tracks numerous document types, each serving a specific purpose in the project lifecycle:
 (1) Certificate of Completion (COC): Most critical document - vendor's formal declaration work is complete, Must be submitted within SLA deadline (typically 7 days after field completion), Triggers QI inspection process, Required before any billing can proceed, Must include: Project details, completion date, work description, contractor signature and seal, Supported by photos showing completed work.
 (2) As-Built Drawings: Show actual installation as built (may differ from design), Required for permanent record and future maintenance, Show exact locations, measurements, and configurations, Must be verified by engineer, Critical for underground work and complex installations, Filed in permanent project records.
 (3) Material Delivery Receipts: Prove materials were delivered to site, Track material accountability and prevent theft, Verify correct materials and quantities received, Required to reconcile material usage vs. billing, Vendor must submit within specified timeframe, Cross-referenced with material specifications.
 (4) Photos (Before, During, After): Before photos: Document site condition before work starts, During photos: Show work in progress, verify methods used, After photos: Show completed installation from multiple angles, Must be clear, well-lit, and show details, Minimum number of photos required varies by project type, Used for remote verification and future reference.
 (5) Test Results and Certifications: Electrical test results (voltage, current, resistance, grounding), Equipment commissioning reports, Safety test certificates, Material test certificates (for cables, poles, transformers, etc.), Calibration certificates for test equipment, Required for technical approval before energization.
 (6) Permits and Clearances: Building permits, Excavation permits, Road opening permits, Utility coordination clearances, Environmental clearances if needed, Local government endorsements, Must be obtained before work can legally proceed.
 (7) Safety Documentation: Risk assessment and safety plan, Toolbox talk records (safety briefings), Personal protective equipment (PPE) records, Incident reports (if any safety issues occurred), Safety inspection checklists, Required by safety regulations and company policy.
 (8) Survey and Site Assessment: Initial site survey report, Site photos and measurements, Obstacle identification, Access assessment, Existing utility identification, Used for planning and design.
 (9) Customer Documents: Customer application or request form, Customer identification and proof of ownership/authority, Signed customer agreements, Customer acceptance of work, Final customer satisfaction confirmation.
 (10) Invoice Supporting Documents: Official invoice from vendor, Tax invoices and receipts, Withholding tax documents, Material cost breakdowns if required, Labor cost documentation, Bank account details for payment.
 (11) Warranty and Guarantees: Warranty certificates for materials used, Guarantee of workmanship from vendor, Manufacturer warranties for equipment, Service level commitments, Valid for specified period (e.g., 12 months).
 (12) Design and Engineering Documents: Approved engineering designs, Specifications and standards referenced, Load calculations, Single line diagrams, Bill of materials (BOM), Technical proposals and solutions. Importance of proper documentation:
 (1) Legal protection - proves work was done correctly and approved,
 (2) Audit trail - shows compliance with procedures and standards,
 (3) Future reference - needed for maintenance, expansion, or troubleshooting,
 (4) Billing justification - supports invoice amounts and contract compliance,
 (5) Quality assurance - demonstrates adherence to specifications,
 (6) Safety compliance - proves safety requirements were met,
 (7) Regulatory requirements - satisfies government and industry regulations,
 (8) Dispute resolution - provides evidence if disagreements arise,
 (9) Performance tracking - enables analysis of vendor performance,
 (10) Knowledge transfer - helps future teams understand what was done. Document submission workflow: Vendor uploads document → System checks file type and size → Document goes to queue for reviewer → Reviewer (Engineer, QI, or Supervisor) checks document → Approved or Rejected with feedback → If rejected, vendor must correct and resubmit → If approved, document moves to permanent record → Document status visible to all stakeholders → Late submissions flagged and may result in penalties. The system tracks: Submission deadline for each document type, Actual submission date, Approval status and date, Who reviewed and approved, Rejection reasons if applicable, How many times document was resubmitted. Missing or late documents block project progression and billing, so timely submission is critical.
knowledge_base.How does automated reminder system work?:
The automated reminder system proactively sends notifications to prevent missed deadlines and keep projects on track:
 (1) Deadline-Based Reminders: System identifies all upcoming deadlines (SLA deadlines, document submissions, inspection dates, payment due dates, task deadlines), Calculates when reminders should be sent (typically at 80% time elapsed, 95% time elapsed, and on the due date), Automatically generates and sends reminders via email, SMS, or in-app notification, Continues sending reminders until action is completed or deadline passes.
 (2) COC Submission Reminders: When project status changes to 'Field Complete': Vendor receives immediate reminder to submit COC, Reminder includes: What needs to be submitted, Deadline date and time, How to submit (link to portal), Required documents and photos, Consequences of late submission. At 80% of deadline (e.g., day 5 of 7-day SLA): 'Friendly reminder' sent to vendor, Shows days remaining, Provides link to quick submission. At 95% of deadline (e.g., day 6.5 of 7): 'Urgent reminder' sent, Subject line marked URGENT, Copy sent to supervisor for awareness, Warns of potential penalties. On deadline day if not submitted: 'Final reminder' sent in the morning, Marked as critical priority, Copy to management for escalation, States deadline is TODAY. After deadline if still not submitted: 'Overdue notice' sent, Penalty process may begin, Daily reminders continue until submitted.
 (3) Inspection Scheduling Reminders: When COC is submitted: QI receives immediate notification to schedule inspection, Reminder includes COC details and deadline to complete inspection (e.g., 3 days). If QI hasn't scheduled after 24 hours: Reminder sent to QI, If still not scheduled after 48 hours: Escalation to supervisor. One day before scheduled inspection: Reminder sent to both QI and vendor, Includes date, time, location, contact information, Checklist of what vendor should prepare. Morning of inspection day: Final reminder to QI and vendor with inspection details.
 (4) Document Review Reminders: When vendor submits document for review: Assigned reviewer receives notification, Document appears in their pending queue. If not reviewed within 1 business day: Reminder sent to reviewer showing overdue items. If still pending after 2 business days (typical review SLA): Escalation to supervisor, Supervisor can reassign to another reviewer if needed.
 (5) Task Assignment Reminders: When task is assigned: Assignee receives immediate notification with task details and deadline. At 50% of time to deadline: Progress reminder sent asking for status update. At 75% of time to deadline: 'Action needed' reminder with days/hours remaining. At 90% of time to deadline: Urgent reminder with copy to supervisor. On deadline day: Final reminder marking task as due TODAY. If task overdue: Daily reminders until completed, automatic escalation to management.
 (6) Payment Reminders: When invoice is issued to vendor: Vendor receives invoice with payment due date. 7 days before payment due: Reminder of upcoming payment, includes invoice number and amount. 3 days before payment due: Another reminder with payment instructions. On payment due date: Payment due today notice. If payment overdue: Daily overdue notices, escalation to collections if severely overdue.
 (7) Penalty Payment Reminders: When penalty is issued: Vendor receives penalty memo with payment deadline (e.g., 30 days). 15 days before deadline: Reminder of penalty and amount due. 7 days before deadline: Urgent payment reminder. 3 days before deadline: Final warning with consequences of non-payment. On deadline: Payment due notice. After deadline: Overdue penalty notices, may affect future project assignments.
 (8) Daily Digest Reminders: For users who opt for digest mode instead of real-time: Morning digest (8 AM): Lists all tasks due today, all overdue items, all items approaching deadlines. Evening digest (5 PM): Summary of what was completed today, what's pending for tomorrow, critical items needing attention. Weekly summary (Monday morning): Week ahead preview, priorities for the week, overdue items from previous week.
 (9) Smart Reminder Features: Frequency limiting - won't spam with too many reminders too close together, Time zone awareness - sends reminders at appropriate local time, Business hours respect - doesn't send at night unless critical, Escalation chain - includes more people as deadline approaches, Actionable links - each reminder includes link to take action directly, Snooze option - users can snooze non-critical reminders, Do Not Disturb mode - users can set quiet hours.
 (10) Reminder Configuration: Administrators can configure: Which events trigger reminders, Timing of reminders (when they're sent), Reminder frequency, Escalation thresholds, Reminder templates and content, Users can configure: Which reminders they want to receive, Preferred delivery method (email, SMS, push), Quiet hours when they don't want reminders, Frequency preferences. Benefits of automated reminders: Reduces missed deadlines by 60-80%, Eliminates need for manual follow-up calls and emails, Ensures consistent treatment of all projects, Provides documentation trail of all notifications sent, Reduces administrative workload, Improves SLA compliance rates, Enables proactive management instead of reactive firefighting. Reminders are logged in the system showing when sent, to whom, and whether the action was completed afterward.
knowledge_base.What is the difference between a Penalty:
Penalties and waivers are two sides of the enforcement system: PENALTIES:
 (1) Definition: Financial deductions from the contract value imposed when vendor fails to meet obligations (missed SLA deadlines, quality failures, safety violations, incomplete documentation).
 (2) Purpose: Encourage vendor compliance and accountability, Compensate for costs and impacts of delays, Deter repeated non-compliance, Maintain fairness (vendors who perform well shouldn't subsidize poor performers).
 (3) When Penalties Apply: SLA breaches (late COC submission, late work completion), Quality issues (work fails inspection, requires re-work), Safety violations (unsafe practices, lack of PPE), Documentation failures (missing documents, late submissions), Repeat offenses (multiple delays or issues on same project or across projects).
 (4) Penalty Amounts: Calculated based on: Violation severity (minor, moderate, critical), Contract value (% of total contract), Delay duration (per day past deadline), Historical precedents (similar past cases), ML model prediction for consistency. Typical ranges: Minor SLA breach (1-2 days late): ₱5,000 - ₱20,000, Moderate delay (3-7 days late): ₱20,000 - ₱100,000, Major delay (>7 days): ₱100,000+ or % of contract value, Quality failure requiring re-work: ₱50,000 - ₱200,000, Safety violation: ₱75,000 - ₱300,000. Maximum cap: Usually limited to 10-20% of contract value.
 (5) Penalty Process: System auto-detects violation, calculates penalty, Penalty issued with formal memo to vendor, Vendor can view in portal with full calculation breakdown, Penalty deducted from invoice when billing occurs, Vendor can pay penalty separately or it's deducted from payment, Unpaid penalties affect future project assignments.
 (6) Impact on Vendor: Reduces payment amount received, Lowers vendor compliance score, Affects future project assignment likelihood, Patterns of penalties may lead to vendor disqualification, Documented in vendor performance history. WAIVERS:
 (1) Definition: Cancellation or reduction of a penalty that was previously issued, based on valid justification or special circumstances.
 (2) Purpose: Recognize legitimate reasons beyond vendor control, Maintain fairness when circumstances were exceptional, Encourage good-faith compliance when vendor made reasonable effort, Balance enforcement with business relationships.
 (3) When Waivers May Be Granted: Force majeure: Typhoons, floods, earthquakes, other natural disasters, Government restrictions or emergency orders, Pandemic lockdowns. Client-caused delays: Customer not available for scheduled work, Customer postponed or changed requirements, Site access denied by customer, Required customer actions not completed. External factors: Permit delays from government agencies, Delays by other utilities (conflict resolution took time), Material shortages beyond vendor's control (global supply issues), Third-party delays that blocked vendor's work. First-time minor violations: New vendor learning the system, First occurrence of a minor issue, Good-faith effort was made but fell slightly short, Vendor has otherwise excellent track record. Errors in penalty calculation: Penalty was based on incorrect facts, SLA deadline was unclear or miscommunicated, Calculation error in penalty amount, Vendor had valid extension that wasn't properly recorded.
 (4) Waiver Process: Vendor submits waiver request through portal or dispute process, Provides detailed justification and supporting evidence: Photos showing site conditions, Weather reports from official sources, Correspondence proving client delays, Third-party statements, Alternative documentation. Request reviewed by supervisor or manager, Evidence evaluated against policy, Decision made: Full waiver (penalty completely cancelled), Partial waiver (penalty reduced but not eliminated), Deny waiver (penalty stands as issued). Vendor notified of decision with explanation, If approved: Penalty removed from records, invoice adjusted, compliance score updated.
 (5) Waiver Documentation: All waivers logged in system with justification, Creates precedent for future similar situations, Waiver statistics tracked (how many, for what reasons), Management reviews waiver rates to ensure policy consistency.
 (6) Limits on Waivers: Repeated delays rarely qualify for waivers (vendor should plan better), Poor planning by vendor not a valid excuse, Vendor's own resource or capacity issues not valid reason, Lack of documentation = difficult to approve waiver, Abuse of waiver process results in stricter enforcement. KEY DIFFERENCES: Penalties = Enforcement tool to ensure compliance, Waivers = Flexibility mechanism for legitimate special circumstances. Good vendors have few penalties and rarely need waivers. Vendors who regularly request waivers may be flagged for performance issues. The goal is balanced system: Strict enough to ensure accountability, Fair enough to recognize genuine exceptions, Consistent enough to treat all vendors equally, Transparent enough that vendors understand the rules and consequences.
knowledge_base.How does the system ensure data accuracy:
The system implements multiple validation and quality control mechanisms:
 (1) Input Validation: Real-time field validation as users type, Required fields marked with asterisk (*), Format checking (dates must be YYYY-MM-DD, phone numbers must be 10-11 digits, emails must contain @, etc.), Range checking (dates cannot be in far future, amounts cannot be negative, etc.), Data type enforcement (numeric fields only accept numbers), Special character restriction in codes and IDs, Duplicate detection (same WO number, project code, vendor code cannot be entered twice), Relationship validation (vendor ID must exist in vendors table before project can be assigned).
 (2) Business Rule Validation: Logical date sequencing (end date must be after start date, completion date must be after COC submission date), Status transitions (project cannot go from Cancelled to Completed), Value limits (contract value must be within reasonable range for project type), Required document validation (certain documents must exist before status change allowed), SLA consistency (SLA deadline must align with project dates), User permission validation (users can only perform actions their role allows).
 (3) Data Entry Assistance: Auto-complete dropdowns for common fields, Pre-populated fields when editing (show current values), Default values for standard selections, Format hints shown in field placeholders (e.g., "YYYY-MM-DD"), Tooltips explaining what each field means, Character counters for fields with length limits, Smart suggestions based on past entries or patterns.
 (4) Bulk Import Validation: Template validation (column headers must match template exactly), Row-by-row validation before import, Comprehensive error reporting: Row number, field name, error description, suggested correction. Preview of data before final import, Ability to cancel import if errors detected, Import results log showing successes and failures.
 (5) Referential Integrity: Foreign key validation (references to other tables must be valid), Cascade rules (deleting a sector shows warning if projects depend on it, deletion prevented or requires reassignment), Orphan prevention (cannot delete vendor if active projects exist), Relationship enforcement in database design.
 (6) Automated Calculations: Penalty amounts calculated by system (reduces human error), SLA deadlines calculated from start dates and rules, Days delayed calculated automatically, Compliance scores calculated by formula, Contract value minus penalties for invoice amount, All calculations logged and auditable.
 (7) Approval Workflows: Multi-level approval for critical changes, Higher authority needed for high-value invoices or waivers, Prevents single person from making major errors unchecked, Approval history tracked.
 (8) Duplicate Detection: System flags potential duplicates based on: Similar project codes, Same work order number, Same location with recent similar work, Same vendor, same sector, same dates. Warning shown before allowing creation, Option to link to existing record instead.
 (9) Data Consistency Checks: Periodic background jobs check for inconsistencies, Flag orphaned records or broken relationships, Identify anomalies (unusually high contract value, very long project duration), Generate exception reports for admin review.
 (10) Audit Trails: All data changes logged with before/after values, User ID, timestamp, and IP address recorded, Changes can be reviewed and reversed if errors found, Suspicious patterns (many changes in short time) flagged.
 (11) Error Messages and User Guidance: Clear, specific error messages (not "An error occurred" but "Contract value cannot exceed ₱10,000,000"), Suggested corrections when possible, Links to help documentation for complex fields, In-app guidance and wizards for complicated processes.
 (12) Data Quality Dashboards: Administrators see data quality metrics: Fields with missing data, Records with validation warnings, Import error rates, Common input mistakes, User error rates by type. Use metrics to identify training needs or process improvements.
 (13) User Training and Standards: Standardized data entry procedures documented, Training for new users on correct data entry, Best practices shared across teams, Common mistakes highlighted in training materials.
 (14) Regular Data Cleanup: Scheduled jobs to clean up: Expired temp records, Incomplete draft entries, Outdated status values, Normalize formatting inconsistencies (capitalization, spacing). Archive old completed projects to keep active data clean.
 (15) Role-Based Data Access: Users only see and edit data relevant to their role, Prevents accidental modification of unrelated records, Reduces complexity of what users need to understand.
 (16) Confirmation Dialogs: Confirmation required before: Deleting any record, Changing critical fields (contract value, vendor assignment), Issuing penalties or waivers, Bulk operations affecting multiple records. "Are you sure?" prevents accidental actions.
 (17) Data Import from External Systems: Validation of data before accepting from integrated systems, Transformation rules to convert formats, Error handling if external data is malformed, Logging of all data received from external sources. Result: The combination of these mechanisms reduces data errors by 90%+ compared to manual systems, maintains high data quality and integrity, provides confidence in reports and analytics, supports regulatory compliance and audit requirements, reduces time spent correcting errors.
